# Education in New Zealand: Summary
New Zealand offers free, compulsory primary and secondary education to citizens and permanent residents from age 5 to 19. The system is organized into 13 year levels, with primary education spanning Years 1–8, including intermediate years, and secondary education covering Years 9–13. Schools operate on a four-term year, and most students stay in school until at least 17. Types of schools include state schools (government-funded, secular), state integrated schools (formerly private schools with a special character, often religious), and private schools (fee-paying, receiving partial government support). State and integrated schools receive funding based on student numbers and socio-economic decile, with additional voluntary donations and, in integrated schools, attendance dues. Disabled students may attend specialist schools until age 21 and are supported through specific government funding schemes.
The national curriculum, divided into The New Zealand Curriculum (NZC) for English-medium and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa (TMoA) for Māori-medium schools, covers eight learning areas, with students specializing from Year 11 onward and working towards the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA), or, in some cases, international qualifications. Māori language education has a distinct history, with significant revival efforts including the establishment of Māori-medium schools (Kura Kaupapa Māori) and programs like kōhanga reo for early childhood immersion. Tertiary education is regulated via a unified qualifications framework and funded through a mix of government grants and student loans/allowances. Despite strong international rankings overall, challenges remain, particularly in maths achievement and in closing gaps between Māori, Pacific, and Pākehā student outcomes. School bullying remains a notable issue, and ongoing reforms aim to address educational equity and improve standards.
